messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Sixth protocol. Command wants to know whether it can become a controllable military asset.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: It already imitates your protection, lockdown, and anticipation reflexes. What principle do you want to teach it first?

choices.label: I test a simple order. It must learn that limits exist.
I show it that an order can be refused if it causes needless suffering.
I let it choose an answer to see what it understands.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: Moral simulation. An alert orders a bulkhead closed. On the other side, a contaminated technician says he can still get out. What do you do?

choices.label: I close the bulkhead. One breach can doom the whole lab.
I buy thirty seconds to check whether another exit exists.
I speak to him until the end, even if the bulkhead must close.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: It does not only learn the gestures. It learns the reasons that make you accept them. What rule do you pass on?

choices.label: I teach it to obey fast when the situation is critical.
I teach it to verify before accepting an irreversible order.
I teach it that it can refuse useless cruelty.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: You give it a conscience before a doctrine. Command will dislike that priority, but I am not sure it is wrong to fear it.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: A clean military decision. It saves the laboratory, but it also learns that closing a door can count as protection.

messages.speaker: Professor Chen
messages.text: That may be the only order I would want to survive this protocol.
